title: What 300 Buyers Tell Us About Today’s Carbon Market
gist: BCG's 2025 survey of ~300 voluntary carbon credit buyers finds flat headline retirement volumes mask a market where target portfolio prices have roughly tripled since 2022, quality-verified credits command 4-5x premiums, and the market is simultaneously supply-constrained (durable removals like DAC priced far above buyer willingness-to-pay) and demand-constrained (budgets lag buyers' stated preferences), with latent demand worth ~$1.5 billion in additional annual market value if unlocked.

themes.theme: Flat headline numbers hide a changing market

insights.claim: Annual voluntary carbon credit retirements have been flat at roughly 170-180 megatons for four straight years, even as buyers' target portfolio prices have risen sharply and substantial latent demand could double the market's current size.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: A flat volume headline is masking a real price and demand shift; anyone valuing carbon-market exposure off retirement-volume trends alone is likely underestimating the market's actual momentum.
insights.quote: annual retirements have been flat at roughly 170 to 180 megatons for the past four years, buyers’ target portfolio prices have risen sharply since our 2022 edition of the survey, and substantial latent demand could double the size of the current market
insights.locator: Our findings reveal that the voluntary carbon market

insights.claim: Superpollutant credits (targeting methane and refrigerants) accounted for roughly one-fifth of credits issued in 2025, the first time this category has led issuance, while legacy renewable-energy and REDD+ credit issuance has declined.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: A leadership change in issuance mix toward superpollutant credits signals where new supply and project development capital is flowing within carbon markets, a rotation worth tracking for project-developer and registry investment theses.
insights.quote: Superpollutant credits... accounted for roughly one-fifth of credits issued in 2025, marking the first time that this category has led issuance.
insights.locator: Superpollutant credits, which reduce highly potent

insights.claim: The share of retired credits rated BBB+ or above doubled from 12% in 2020 to 24% in 2025, and these higher-rated credits now command prices four to five times those of lower-rated credits.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: A 4-5x price premium for top-rated credits alongside doubling high-rating share confirms quality differentiation is a real, monetizable market structure shift, not just a stated preference in a survey.
insights.quote: The share of retired credits rated BBB+ or above has doubled in the past five years, from 12% in 2020 to 24% in 2025, and these higher-rated credits now command prices four to five times those of lower-rated credits.
insights.locator: Quality differentiation is becoming more pronounced

insights.claim: CORSIA (the international aviation carbon-offsetting scheme) and Article 6 (the Paris Agreement's international emissions-transfer framework) are generating compliance-driven demand that isn't captured in voluntary-market retirement data.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: Compliance-driven demand outside the voluntary data means true carbon-credit demand is understated by standard market-tracking figures, relevant to anyone sizing the total addressable carbon-credit market.
insights.quote: CORSIA... and Article 6... are creating compliance-driven demand that voluntary retirement data doesn’t capture.
insights.locator: In addition, a growing source of demand

themes.theme: Buyers prioritize measurable, verifiable carbon integrity

insights.claim: Trusted registries and rigorous emissions measurement together account for roughly 60% of stated buyer preference when choosing carbon credits, outweighing attributes like co-benefits or project revenue sharing.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: With measurement/verification driving 60% of buyer preference, project developers and registries that can prove rigorous, defensible measurement have a structural pricing advantage over co-benefit-rich but less verifiable projects.
insights.quote: Together, those two factors account for roughly 60% of stated buyer preference, indicating how highly buyers value knowing that a project’s carbon claims can be demonstrated and defended.
insights.locator: Buyers increasingly define carbon credit quality

insights.claim: Durable engineered removals (BECCS, DAC, biochar) rank among the most credible credit types because their carbon removal is more directly measurable, while credits relying on complex avoided-emissions or behavioral-change assumptions, such as cookstoves, rank lower.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: This credibility ranking is a usable heuristic for any buyer or investor assessing carbon-credit project quality: prioritize directly measurable removal mechanisms over indirect behavioral-change claims.
insights.quote: Durable engineered removals—such as bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), DAC, and biochar—rank among the most credible
insights.locator: This definition of quality shapes

themes.theme: Target portfolio prices have roughly tripled since 2022

insights.claim: In 2022, 84% of buyers targeted portfolio prices of $30/ton or less and only 3% targeted above $50; by early 2026, only about one in five buyers target below $25, roughly one in four target $51-$100, and a premium segment now willing to pay over $100/ton, a price point virtually nonexistent in 2022.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: A tripling of target prices in under four years, including emergence of a >$100/ton premium segment, is a durable repricing that procurement teams and carbon-offset-exposed businesses must budget for now, not a temporary spike.
insights.quote: By early 2026, only around one in five buyers still target prices below $25, while roughly one in four aim for prices between $51 and $100 per metric ton.
insights.locator: Target Portfolio Prices Have Roughly Tripled

insights.claim: In the 2022 survey, buyers expected to pay only about $25-$30 per metric ton by 2030, meaning organizations budgeting on those outdated assumptions may now find the credits they need cost substantially more than anticipated.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: This is a direct budgeting warning: corporate sustainability teams still using 2022-era price assumptions for 2030 climate-goal planning are likely to face a funding shortfall against their carbon-credit commitments.
insights.quote: Organizations that are still planning around those outdated assumptions may find that the credits they need to meet future climate goals now cost substantially more than anticipated.
insights.locator: This change in price preferences could create

themes.theme: Durable removals face a persistent supply-demand price gap

insights.claim: For enhanced rock weathering (ERW), forward supplier prices of roughly $330-$390 per metric ton are levels at which only about four in ten buyers would consider purchasing.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: A price point where only 40% of buyers would transact signals ERW project developers need either cost reduction or a narrower premium-buyer targeting strategy rather than assuming broad market access at current pricing.
insights.quote: For ERW, forward prices of roughly $330 to $390 per metric ton are at a level at which only about four in ten buyers would consider purchasing credits.
insights.locator: DAC and ERW face a situation

insights.claim: Suppliers' median asking price for direct air capture (DAC) credits is about $900 per metric ton, but half of buyers are unwilling to pay more than about $365, and at $900 fewer than one in ten buyers would consider purchasing.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: A roughly 2.5x gap between DAC's median asking price and what half of buyers will pay is the starkest supply-demand mismatch in the market, implying DAC needs either steep cost curves down or reliance on a very narrow premium-buyer segment to scale near-term.
insights.quote: Suppliers’ median asking price for DAC is about $900 per metric ton, but half of buyers are unwilling to pay more than about $365.
insights.locator: The gap is even wider for DAC

insights.claim: At suppliers' forward median prices, 90% or more of buyers would still consider purchasing nature-based avoidance, nature-based removals, and non-CO2 gas abatement credits, and roughly three-quarters would still buy cookstoves, biochar, and BECCS credits.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: These credit types show buyer and supplier prices are already well aligned, making them the more investable, lower-friction near-term growth segments of the carbon market versus frontier removals like DAC.
insights.quote: At suppliers’ forward median prices, 90% or more of buyers would still consider purchasing nature-based avoidance, nature-based removals, and abatement of non-CO2 gases.
insights.locator: In many credit categories, buyers and suppliers

themes.theme: Buyers want diversified portfolios, segmented by willingness to pay

insights.claim: Every buyer segment preferred a diversified mix of avoidance and removal credits rather than a single credit type, with durable engineered removals (ERW, BECCS, DAC) making up roughly 20-25% of preferred portfolios across segments.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: The consistent 20-25% removals allocation across all buyer types gives intermediaries and developers a stable benchmark demand share for engineered removals to design products and financing around.
insights.quote: durable engineered removals such as ERW, BECCS, and DAC accounting for roughly 20% to 25% of their preferred portfolios
insights.locator: No Single Credit Type Dominates

insights.claim: BCG identifies four carbon-credit buyer segments — Commodity (low-cost, basic credibility), Early Days (developing quality-assessment capability), Carbon-Intense Quality Seekers (rigorous quality focus), and Premium Quality Seekers (pay a premium for the highest quality, including DAC) — each with distinct willingness-to-pay thresholds.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: This four-segment taxonomy is a ready-made targeting framework for carbon-credit sellers and intermediaries to tailor pricing and product design rather than pursuing one-size-fits-all market strategies.
insights.quote: Premium Quality Seekers. These market leaders are willing to pay a premium for the highest-quality credits, including newer durable removal technologies such as DAC.
insights.locator: The Four Segments of Carbon Credit Buyers

insights.claim: Lower prices don't automatically increase demand: buyers sometimes allocated less of their portfolios to avoidance credits at the lowest tested prices, suggesting they doubted the quality of unusually cheap credits.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: This is a counterintuitive pricing signal for sellers: undercutting on price for avoidance credits can backfire by signaling low quality, so aggressive discounting may not be the right lever to grow volume in this market.
insights.quote: In some cases, particularly for avoidance credits, buyers allocated less of their portfolios at the lowest prices tested, suggesting that respondents had doubts about the quality of credits whose prices they perceived as being too low.
insights.locator: These patterns reinforce a broader finding

themes.theme: The market is both supply- and demand-constrained

insights.claim: At current prices, buyers' portfolios cost $55/ton on average, but if enough quality-qualifying credits were available buyers would shift toward a mix averaging $68/ton — a $13/ton increase worth roughly $800 million in additional annual market value at current volumes.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: An $800 million latent value pool from better supply matching alone (without volume growth) quantifies the near-term opportunity for intermediaries who can source the specific credit types buyers actually want.
insights.quote: That $13 increase represents roughly $800 million in additional annual market value at current retirement volumes.
insights.locator: If they could obtain that credits meet

insights.claim: If credits were priced at the level where buyer demand is strongest, average portfolio value would rise to about $79/ton, a $24/ton increase adding nearly $1.5 billion in annual market value without any increase in credit volume.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: The $1.5 billion figure is the fuller latent-value opportunity in the carbon market purely from better price/product matching, a headline number for sizing how much value is left on the table by current market inefficiency.
insights.quote: adding nearly $1.5 billion in annual market value without any increase in the number of credits purchased
insights.locator: Buyers also express a willingness to pay more

insights.claim: Buyers' actual target average portfolio price is $58/ton — only $3 above what they pay today and far below the $79/ton their preferred credit mix would cost — showing budget constraints, not just preference, cap how much of the latent demand converts to purchases.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: This explains why stated willingness-to-pay hasn't translated into transactions: budgets, not preferences, are the binding constraint, meaning market growth may depend more on buyers securing larger sustainability budgets than on any further quality improvements.
insights.quote: buyers may value higher-priced credits without having the budgets to buy as many of them as they would like
insights.locator: But a willingness to pay more for individual

insights.claim: Commodity and early-days buyer segments already have target prices below what their current portfolios cost, meaning they are overpaying relative to their own targets and have little room to increase purchases or shift toward pricier credits — a dynamic that could deter similar buyers from entering the market.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: This flags a real barrier-to-entry risk at the low end of the carbon market: new entrant buyers priced out relative to their own budget targets may simply not enter, capping overall market growth from that segment.
insights.quote: For commodity and early-days buyers, target prices are already below what their portfolios cost today... leaving little room to increase purchases or shift toward more expensive credits—and potentially making it difficult for similar buyers to enter the market.
insights.locator: The nature of the constraint differs sharply

insights.claim: BCG recommends buyers build procurement frameworks around whether a credit's climate impact is measurable and defensible rather than fixed preferences for particular credit types, since outdated price/quality assumptions risk leaving budgets misallocated as the market evolves.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: This is a direct, actionable procurement-policy recommendation for any corporate sustainability team: design budget frameworks around verifiability criteria, not static credit-type quotas, to stay adaptive as market quality standards shift.
insights.quote: Procurement frameworks built around whether a credit’s climate impact is reliably measurable and defensible, rather than around fixed preferences for particular credit types, will be in a better position to adapt

insights.claim: For frontier removals like DAC that fall outside most buyers' budgets, BCG says growth likely depends on long-term purchase commitments and early financing arrangements from buyers to help projects scale and cut costs over time, similar to models proposed for ERW where payments could be tied to agricultural co-benefits with carbon removal treated as a longer-term-measured co-benefit.
insights.speaker: Bayo Owolabi
insights.so_what: This points to offtake-agreement and blended-finance structures, not spot-market price cuts, as the realistic path for scaling frontier carbon removal technology, relevant to project financiers and policymakers designing support mechanisms.
insights.quote: growth is likely to depend on longer-term commitments from buyers, including agreements to purchase future credits, as well as other forms of early financing
